Unveiling Solubilization Mechanisms of Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents in Triazole Fungicides: COSMO-RS Calculations and Screening for Eco-Friendly, High-Efficiency Pesticide Systems
Juan Wang, Fengmao Liu,* Qingrong Peng,* Xianzhao Zhang, Zhiqiang Gao, Peirong Zhang, Wenzhuo Wang, and Jing Sun
Cite This: ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2024, 12, 13149-13162 Read Online

ABSTRACT: Enhancing the dissolution of lipophilic agrochemicals is paramount for addressing agricultural environmental pollution and improving utilization efficiency. This study introduced a novel methodology to enhance pesticide solubility by integrating theoretical calculations, targeted design, and high-throughput screening for the development of sustainable solvents. Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs) optimized for pesticide formulation were systematically designed and selectively filtered from 1768 species, exhibiting exceptional solubility for triazole fungicides identified through the conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS). Experimental results demonstrated a significant increase in solubility relative to water, ranging from 2.8 to 3.6 × 10⁵ times. Molecular dynamics simulations, quantitative calculations, and property measurements elucidated van der Waals and hydrogen bonding interactions as the dominant roles of the solubilization mechanisms. Furthermore, the novel eco-friendly pesticide system, integrating triadimefon with three NADESs, exhibited a 0.87 times increase in inhibitory activity against Fusarium graminearum, accompanied by a 15.6% reduction in equilibrium surface tension and a 58.1% decrease in contact angle on wheat leaves compared to commercial emulsifiable concentrate (EC). ## INTRODUCTION Pesticides play a pivotal role in mitigating crop pests and diseases, enhancing crop yield, and supporting modern agricultural development.1-3 Despite their significant contributions, the high hydrophobicity of pesticide active ingredients (AIs) necessitates the extensive use of organic solvents in both manufacturing and application processes, resulting in substantial volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emissions.4,5 Studies indicated that agricultural sources contribute to approximately 14% of anthropogenic VOCs emissions.1 The inherent challenges of poor water solubility and low foliar retention rate of active ingredients compel increased usage, leading to elevated levels of aromatic hydrocarbon discharge into the environment and subsequent environmental pollution and ecological damage.6-8 Hence, there is a critical need to design novel, environmentally friendly, naturally derived, and tunable green solvents. Moreover, the development of sustainable pesticide formulation systems is imperative to
curb organic solvent emissions, optimize pesticide utilization, and enhance overall environmental safety and human health.

The identification of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) represents a significant advancement in green chemistry. DESs, a groundbreaking solvent system initially proposed by Abbott et al.⁹ in 2003, are characterized as low-melting-point mixtures with specific stoichiometric ratios of hydrogen bonding donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bonding acceptors (HBAs), connected through hydrogen bonding. These mixtures exhibit considerably lower melting points than either individual component, demonstrating high thermal stability,

NADESS, recognized as "designer solvents," are environ- mentally friendly, pose lower toxicity risks, and find widespread applications across various fields.12-16 Notably, NADESS exhibit significant potential in enhancing drug solubility, 17-19 permeability, 20,21 and stability 19,22,23 due to their exceptional solubilization capabilities across a broad spectrum of compounds.

Despite the well-established applications of NADESs in pharmaceuticals, their utilization in pesticide formulation remains at an early stage of exploration. Dunan et al.24 investigated formulations containing malic acid/sorbitol/water 1:1:3 and malic acid/serine/water 1:1:3, showcasing high solubility to the phytocide ethylene oxide. These formulations, when used as essential oils, not only minimized damage to the target plant but also exhibited increased tobacco louse mortality and more gradual release kinetics, suggesting the potential for effective and sustained pest control. In a separate study, Wang et al.25 designed a system involving DESs and mesoporous silica nanoparticles, demonstrating that DESs can influence the arrangement and spatial structure of lignin and cellulose. This modulation enhances the leaf barrier function, improves permeability, and facilitates the distribution and transport of pesticides within the plant. Additionally, prior investigations have confirmed the robust solubilizing capacity of quaternary DESs for highly hydrophobic pesticide AIs.26 These findings introduce innovative possibilities for NADESs to replace hazardous solvents in traditional pesticide formulations, paving the way for the development of green and efficient pesticide-like systems.

An inherent feature of NADESs is their designability, a characteristic that broadens their application spectrum while simultaneously introducing increased complexity and selection costs. The conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) model, introduced by Klamt et al.,$^{27}$ stands out as a predictive model amalgamating quantum chemistry and statistical thermodynamics. This model quantifies thermodynamic properties and associated parameters without relying on experimental data, making it a valuable tool for solvent design and screening across various domains.$^{28–32}$ The model's reliability in predicting outcomes not only mitigates the need for extensive trial-and-error approaches but also enhances research efficiency and accuracy.

Triazole fungicides (TFs) have gained widespread applica- tion in agriculture and industry, constituting 30% of the global fungicide market, attributed to their exceptional characteristics encompassing broad-spectrum efficacy, high efficiency, pro- longed persistence, and commendable systemic properties.33 However, the intrinsic ultralow solubility in water necessitates the formulation of TFs into conventional dosage forms such as emulsifiable concentrate (EC). In these formulations, the inclusion of cosolvents not only introduces their own contaminants but also has the potential to elevate environ- mental toxicity,34,35 reproductive metabolism toxicity,36,37 and induce endocrine-disrupting effects38,39 associated with TFs. These concerns pose significant threats to human health and environmental well-being.

In this investigation, six TFs (Table S1) served as the target compounds. Specifically, for triadimefon (TDF), the system-atic design of NADESs involved a comprehensive selection of natural constituents, including organic alcohols, terpenes, organic bases, organic amines, amino acids, and other pertinent components, utilizing the COSMO-RS methodology. The identification of suitable NADESs was facilitated by evaluating their solubility capacities, with the reliability of the simulation calculations validated through experimental solubility measure-ments. Furthermore, the solubilization mechanism of TDF by NADESS was thoroughly elucidated by integrating COSMO-RS with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Additionally, the applicability of the designed screening approach was validated by extending the solubility measurements to five other TFs: myclobutanil, hexaconazole, tebuconazole, difeno-conazole, and propiconazole. Subsequently, three environ-mentally friendly formulations of TDF based on NADESs were developed and systematically compared with commercial EC concerning in vitro activity, foliar adhesion effects, biocompat-ibility, and cytotoxicity.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS **Materials.** The components of NADESs involved in this study shown in Table S2 (purity, 98%) were procured from Sigma-Aldrich Trading Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Six TF technicals (purity, 97%) were sourced from Changshu Hengyao New Material Co., Ltd. (Jiangshu, China). Methanol and acetonitrile (chromatography grade) were acquired from Meridian Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).

Dissolution and Mechanism Exploration. Design and Screen- ing of Solvents. The screening of NADESs was conducted in conjunction with the COSMO-RS design. Initially, TURBOMOLE software (version 21.0.0) was utilized, with def-TZVP chosen as the computational basis set and the computational temperature set at 25 °C. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to optimize the TFs AIs to their lowest energy states, generating corresponding energy files (molecular structures of TFs and NADESs components were retrieved from the PubChem database). Sub- sequently, single-point calculations were performed by using the COSMO continuous solvatization method. The surface shielding charge (σ) density distribution was calculated, and the relevant information was stored in a cosmo file, applicable in BIOVIA COSMOtherm software (version 22.0.0). The COSMOtherm software contains a COSMObase with components of NADESs. Utilizing the "multisolvent" panel in COSMOtherm, the solubility of target pesticides in the designed NADESs was calculated by determining the molar ratios of the components. Additionally, COSMOtherm computed the fusion properties of individual components of the screened NADESs based on the solubility parameter. These properties were utilized in predictive modeling of solid–liquid equilibrium (SLE) plots by COSMOtherm, determining the eutectic melting temperature as a crucial parameter for assessing the feasibility of NADESs preparation under room-temperature conditions.

Preparation of NADESs. Preparation of NADESs was conducted using a heating and stirring method. 40,41 Following the COSMO-therm-designed and screened NADESs combinations, components were meticulously weighed in a 1:1 molar ratio and mixed in a 250 mL round-bottomed flask. The mixture was then subjected to heating and stirring under a water bath at 70–80 °C, facilitated by a magnetic stirrer (DF-101S, China), until a clarified and transparent liquid was achieved. Subsequently, the solution was cooled to room temperature, allowing it to stand for 24 h while maintaining its clarified and transparent state, indicating the successful preparation of NADESs.

Dissolution Mechanism Studies. The dissolution mechanism was elucidated through MD simulations using GROMACS 2021.6 software suite. 43,44 The GROMOS96 54a7 United-Atom force field was employed to describe all molecules, 45 and the parameters for

Application of TDF-NADESs Formulations. Preparation and Stability Assessment of TDF-NADESS. Referring to commercial EC formulations, TFs based on NADESs formulations with varying concentrations were separately prepared. The storage stability at elevated temperature of the AIs in six TFs was evaluated following the CIPAC MT46.3. These formulations were sealed in glass bottles and subjected to thermal storage in a constant temperature chamber at 54 ± 2 °C for 14 days. Subsequently, the samples were retrieved, placed in a desiccator, and cooled to room temperature, and the mass fraction of the AIs was determined.

In Vitro Activity Assessment. The in vitro inhibitory activity of TDF-NADES systems against *Fusarium graminearum* was evaluated using the mycelial growth rate method. Evaluation of Cytotoxicity. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the CCK-8 assay. L929 cells obtained from the Shanghai Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences were inoculated into 96-well plates and cultured for 24 h. After the culture medium was discarded, the cells were rinsed twice with phosphate buffered saline (PBS). Equal volumes of TDF-NADESS and EC at 10 mg/kg were added to the experimental group, while the control group received only the culture medium. After 24 h of continued incubation in the dark, the culture solution was removed, and the wells were rinsed twice with PBS. 100 µL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and placed in the incubator for 2 h. ## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION **COSMO-RS Screening Results.** A comprehensive screening process employing COSMO-RS was conducted using a diverse set of 53 organic alcohols, terpenoids, organic bases, organic amines, and amino acids as HBAs and 34 organic amines and amino acids as HBDs (Table S2). These components were combined in a 1:1 molar ratio, resulting in the generation of 1768 NADESs. The solubilization potential of these NADESs toward TDF was predicted, utilizing TDF as a model drug (Figure 1a). The heat map visually represents the solubility capacity, with color transitions from red to blue indicating a gradual decrease in solubilization efficacy. Notably, NADESs with terpenoids and long-chain alkanols as HBAs, coupled with polyacids and long-chain alkanoic acids as HBDs, demonstrated superior solubilization capabilities. Conversely, NADESS containing amino acids exhibited diminished solubilization efficiency.

Based on the shielding charge density (σ), the σ-profile can be categorized into three regions, where -0.0082 < σ < 0.0082 e/Å² represents the nonpolar region, σ > 0.0082 e/Å² corresponds to the HBA region, and σ < 0.0082 e/Å² designates the HBD region. 32,52 Generally, compounds exhibiting pronounced peaks in the nonpolar region tend to exhibit enhanced solubility when paired with NADESs sharing a similar peak distribution. The actual solubility measurements are presented in Figure 2a, revealing a notable enhancement in NADES solubility, ranging from approximately 2.80 × 10³ to 1.02 × 10⁴-fold compared to TDF solubility in water. Considering the pronounced acidic nature of LaA (Table S3), potentially limiting its practical applicability, our focus shifted to investigating NADESs based on DA in subsequent analyses. The solubilization capability of various DA-based

Additionally, as illustrated in Figure 3b, the densities of three NADESSs were all lower than that of water at 20 °C, consistent with the general observation that the density of most hydrophobic DESs is lower than that of water. 54 The lower density may be attributed to the presence of DA, increasing compressibility and resulting in augmented free volume and a decrease in density. Similarly, with the rise in temperature, weakened intermolecular interaction forces and expanded intermolecular voids in NADESs lead to an increase in molecular volume and a subsequent decrease in density. 55

The melting points ($T_m$) of NADESs were consistently lower than those of their individual components. The substantial interactions between HBAs and HBDs contributed to the reduced $T_m$ observed in eutectics.56 A lower $T_m$ increased the practical application range of NADESs. Table 2

illustrates that NADESS T_m was influenced by various factors, including different HBDs, the mode of interaction with decanoic acid, and lattice energy. Furthermore, the refractive index, a crucial physical property of NADESS, provided insights into molecular interactions between HBAs and HBDs in the NADES composition. 56 The molar refractive indices of the three NADESs in Table 2 align with their solubility capabilities. As refractive indices decreased, the strengthening of hydrogen bonding interactions between components impacted the solubility of TFs.

Polarity stands out as a critical property of NADESs, playing a pivotal role in solvent solubility. ⁵⁷ One widely adopted measure of polarity is the Kamlet–Taft solute discoloration parameter, which gauges the polarity/polarizability, HBD capacity, and HBA capacity of NADESs through the measurement of π*, α, and β values, respectively, using a dye indicator.⁴² As outlined in Table 2, correlating polarity parameters with the observed solubilization ability for TDF, a relationship between the solubilization capacity for TFs and the Kamlet–Taft parameter can be established; specifically, higher HBA ability (β value) with lower polar π* value and α value indicates a more potent solubilization capacity.

primary focus was on exploring the fundamental properties of NADESs composed of DA and Ter. Generally, the mobility of NADESs undergoes gradual changes, corresponding to variations in the ratio. In essence, higher DA ratios result in lower intermolecular interactions with Ter, leading to increased mobility. The optimization of this ratio holds potential for practical solvent carrier applications. Simulations were performed for Ter-DA with molar ratios of 1:1, 2:1, and 3:1. Diffusion coefficients for each substance in these three eutectic solvents were calculated, revealing that the mixtures with a 1:1 ratio exhibited the highest mobility (Table 3). Additionally, the densities of these solvents showed relatively small deviations from the experimental results, validating the force field parameters for these molecules.
Subsequently, the determination of free energies of solubilization of TDF in each solvent was carried out through

free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations to comprehend the impact of differences on solubility (Figure S1). In alignment with the experimental findings, the free energy of TDF dissolution gradually decreased with an increase in the Ter ratio in the solvent. Specifically, the Ter and DA ratio of 1:1 yielded the lowest free energy of dissolution (Table 3), signifying optimal solubilization of TDF in this solvent. In FEP calculations, Coulombic and van der Waals interactions were decoupled sequentially (Figure 4), elucidating the contribution of each interaction. The analysis revealed that van der Waals interactions predominantly governed dissolution; however, the decline in free energy of dissolution from 1:1 to 2:1 was primarily steered by Coulombic interactions.

In-depth exploration of the interaction mode and strength between TDF and solvent molecules was conducted through quantum chemical calculations on a series of solvent–solvent dimers. These dimers were constructed via conformational searching for each monomer. Quantitative analysis of the molecular surface electrostatic potential (ESP) revealed consistently low values, even at the maximum or minimum points of the ESP (Figure 5a). Binding energies were computed, and three geometries representing the most stable binding configurations between TDF and each solvent molecule were selected for further analysis. **Stability Assessment.** Pesticides necessitate a certain duration between their production and utilization. To ensure product quality, the stability of AIs in formulations is typically evaluated through hot storage stability tests. The thermal storage stability of TDF, along with myclobutanil, hexaconazole, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, and propiconazole, was assessed when it was dissolved in Ter-DA, Men-DA, DAch-DA, and Oct-DA using the CIPAC method. Both high and low concentrations maintained the stability of AIs, with content degradation before and after storage remaining below 5%. The formulations based on NADESs demonstrated the capacity to sustain the stability of product activity over a defined period (Figure S2).

In Vitro Activity Evaluation. F. graminearum stands as the primary pathogen responsible for wheat scab, a highly destructive and challenging-to-control disease in agricultural production. Varied concentrations of TDF in Ter-DA, Men-DA, DAch-DA, and commercial EC were subjected to inhibitory activity assessments against F. graminearum, with results illustrated in Figure 6. The colony images in Figure 6a, captured at 72 h, demonstrate effective inhibition of F. graminearum growth across concentrations ranging from 6.25 to 200 mg/L. Figure 6b showed images of colony growth at different times under treatment with the concentration applied in the field (200 mg/L). The concentration-dependent inhibitory effects of TDF formulations were evident, showing a substantial increase in inhibition rates with increasing concentrations (Figure 6c-e). TDF-NADESs exhibited significantly higher inhibitory effects compared to EC. For instance, at 24 h, the inhibition rate for TDF EC was 53.2% at the lowest concentration (6.25 mg/L) and 92.6% at the highest concentration (200 mg/L). In contrast, TDF-NADESs achieved rates of 60.2 and 93.7%, respectively, indicating increased bactericidal activity in the presence of NADESs.

Furthermore, the inhibitory effect at concentrations below 100 mg/L gradually decreased with an extended treatment time. However, at higher concentrations, not only did the inhibitory effect remain unaffected but it also exhibited an enhancement. EC50 values at 24 h for EC, Ter-DA, Men-DA, and DAch-DA were 5.252, 3.864, 4.589, and 3.848 mg/L, respectively, indicating superior activities of TDF-NADES formulations (Table 4). In conclusion, TDF-NADES formulations exhibited excellent in vitro bacterial inhibitory
activities, showcasing significant potential for practical applications in agriculture.

Adhesion of TDF-NADESS on Wheat Leaves. The adherence of droplets to wheat leaves is pivotal for effective pesticide distribution and utilization. ⁶⁰ Figure 7a depicts the EST of TDF-NADESS and EC drops at varying dilutions, with field applications typically conducted at a 1000-fold dilution. At this concentration, the EST of the TDF-NADESs liquid was 14.5–15.6% lower than EC at the field application dilution, proving that the presence of NADESs contributed to a reduction in the EST of the formulation system. Additionally, the wettability of the formulation system on wheat leaves was evaluated through DCA measurements. As shown in Figure 7b, wheat leaf surfaces exhibited high hydrophobicity, evidenced by water's minimal wetting, with a DCA changing from 128 to 127° over 120 s. At a 1000-fold dilution, NADESs-based formulations exhibited 31.6–58.1% lower DCA, facilitating enhanced wetting and faster spreading on wheat leaves compared to EC.

As shown in Figure 7c, the adhesion work of EC was 14.9 mJ/m², while Ter-DA, Men-DA, and DAch-DA exhibited higher values of 35.3, 28.2, and 30.4 mJ/m², respectively. This underscores that TDF-NADESs formulations exhibited supe- rior adhesion to hydrophobic wheat leaves, enhancing solution utilization.

The hydrophobic component of wheat leaves primarily comprises a waxy layer, predominantly composed of sterols with chain lengths ranging from C20 to C32, where C28 is the dominant component. SEM revealed a microstructure with numerous folds, trichome structures, and a dense arrangement of waxy lamellar crystals, accentuating the leaf hydrophobicity (Figure 7f). The intermolecular interactions between C28 sterols and NADESs and conventional solvents (benzene, toluene, and xylene) were calculated using a COMO-RS simulation (Figure 7e,g). The results indicated that NADESs exhibited stronger van der Waals forces and readily formed intermolecular hydrogen bonds with C28 sterols. This suggests that TDF-NADESs formulations hold promising applications in wheat and similar crops. Leveraging the morphology, microstructure, and composition of target crop leaves, cosolvents for active ingredients can be designed and screened using COSMO-RS, providing a simplified and effective approach for future pesticide formulation design and preparation.

Wheat, being highly susceptible to environ- mental variations, experiences growth inhibitory effects due to external environmental resistance and stress factors. 32 Assess- ing the biosafety of TDF-NADESS involves measuring wheat growth indicators. CONCLUSIONS In this comprehensive investigation, COSMO-RS was utilized for the innovative design and high-throughput screening of novel NADESs with a superior solubilizing capacity for TDF. The reliability of COSMO-RS computational screening was corroborated by determining the actual solubility. The solubility of screened NADESs for TFs was enhanced by 2.8 × 10³ to 3.6 × 10⁵ times relative to water. This substantiated the universality of the screened NADESs against TDF for various TFs. Combining MD simulations, quantitative calculations, and properties, the critical factors and sites affecting the solvency of NADESs on TFs were identified as the hydrogen bonding between the triazole ring and hydroxyl group as well as the van der Waals force between benzene rings, which provided a foundational theoretical framework for future solvent design and screening endeavors. In addition, the properties of NADESs, such as viscosity, density, and polarity, also have a certain influence on their solubilization ability. Moreover, compared to conventional EC, the creation of eco-friendly TDF-NADESs formulation demonstrated enhanced in vitro inhibitory activity, superior adhesion, wetting abilities of wheat leaves, and lower EC₅₀ against F. graminearum. The interaction between NADESs components and leaf surface substances was systematically explored through calculations and characterization. Additionally, the pesticide systems of NADESs formulations exhibited diminished effects on wheat crop growth, lower cytotoxicity, and commendable biosafety. Leveraging the advantageous features of NADESs, such as natural components, high solubility, design flexibility, and the capacity to enhance pesticide utilization, holds tremendous promise for elevating pesticide efficiency, mitigating environmental pollution, and ushering in a new era of sustainable and efficient pesticides.

NADESS, recognized as "designer solvents," are environ- mentally friendly, pose lower toxicity risks, and find widespread applications across various fields.12-16 Notably, NADESS exhibit significant potential in enhancing drug solubility, 17-19 permeability, 20,21 and stability 19,22,23 due to their exceptional solubilization capabilities across a broad spectrum of compounds. Despite the well-established applications of NADESs in pharmaceuticals, their utilization in pesticide formulation remains at an early stage of exploration. Dunan et al.24 investigated formulations containing malic acid/sorbitol/water 1:1:3 and malic acid/serine/water 1:1:3, showcasing high solubility to the phytocide ethylene oxide. These formulations, when used as essential oils, not only minimized damage to the target plant but also exhibited increased tobacco louse mortality and more gradual release kinetics, suggesting the potential for effective and sustained pest control. In a separate study, Wang et al.25 designed a system involving DESs and mesoporous silica nanoparticles, demonstrating that DESs can influence the arrangement and spatial structure of lignin and cellulose. This modulation enhances the leaf barrier function, improves permeability, and facilitates the distribution and transport of pesticides within the plant. Additionally, prior investigations have confirmed the robust solubilizing capacity of quaternary DESs for highly hydrophobic pesticide AIs.26 These findings introduce innovative possibilities for NADESs to replace hazardous solvents in traditional pesticide formulations, paving the way for the development of green and efficient pesticide-like systems. An inherent feature of NADESs is their designability, a characteristic that broadens their application spectrum while simultaneously introducing increased complexity and selection costs. The conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) model, introduced by Klamt et al.,$^{27}$ stands out as a predictive model amalgamating quantum chemistry and statistical thermodynamics. This model quantifies thermodynamic properties and associated parameters without relying on experimental data, making it a valuable tool for solvent design and screening across various domains.$^{28–32}$ The model's reliability in predicting outcomes not only mitigates the need for extensive trial-and-error approaches but also enhances research efficiency and accuracy. Triazole fungicides (TFs) have gained widespread applica- tion in agriculture and industry, constituting 30% of the global fungicide market, attributed to their exceptional characteristics encompassing broad-spectrum efficacy, high efficiency, pro- longed persistence, and commendable systemic properties.33 However, the intrinsic ultralow solubility in water necessitates the formulation of TFs into conventional dosage forms such as emulsifiable concentrate (EC). In these formulations, the inclusion of cosolvents not only introduces their own contaminants but also has the potential to elevate environ- mental toxicity,34,35 reproductive metabolism toxicity,36,37 and induce endocrine-disrupting effects38,39 associated with TFs. These concerns pose significant threats to human health and environmental well-being. In this investigation, six TFs (Table S1) served as the target compounds. Specifically, for triadimefon (TDF), the system-atic design of NADESs involved a comprehensive selection of natural constituents, including organic alcohols, terpenes, organic bases, organic amines, amino acids, and other pertinent components, utilizing the COSMO-RS methodology. The identification of suitable NADESs was facilitated by evaluating their solubility capacities, with the reliability of the simulation calculations validated through experimental solubility measure-ments. Furthermore, the solubilization mechanism of TDF by NADESS was thoroughly elucidated by integrating COSMO-RS with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Additionally, the applicability of the designed screening approach was validated by extending the solubility measurements to five other TFs: myclobutanil, hexaconazole, tebuconazole, difeno-conazole, and propiconazole. Subsequently, three environ-mentally friendly formulations of TDF based on NADESs were developed and systematically compared with commercial EC concerning in vitro activity, foliar adhesion effects, biocompat-ibility, and cytotoxicity. ## MATERIALS AND METHODS **Materials.** The components of NADESs involved in this study shown in Table S2 (purity, 98%) were procured from Sigma-Aldrich Trading Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Six TF technicals (purity, 97%) were sourced from Changshu Hengyao New Material Co., Ltd. (Jiangshu, China). Methanol and acetonitrile (chromatography grade) were acquired from Meridian Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Dissolution and Mechanism Exploration. Design and Screen- ing of Solvents. The screening of NADESs was conducted in conjunction with the COSMO-RS design. Initially, TURBOMOLE software (version 21.0.0) was utilized, with def-TZVP chosen as the computational basis set and the computational temperature set at 25 °C. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to optimize the TFs AIs to their lowest energy states, generating corresponding energy files (molecular structures of TFs and NADESs components were retrieved from the PubChem database). Sub- sequently, single-point calculations were performed by using the COSMO continuous solvatization method. The surface shielding charge (σ) density distribution was calculated, and the relevant information was stored in a cosmo file, applicable in BIOVIA COSMOtherm software (version 22.0.0). The COSMOtherm software contains a COSMObase with components of NADESs. Utilizing the "multisolvent" panel in COSMOtherm, the solubility of target pesticides in the designed NADESs was calculated by determining the molar ratios of the components. Additionally, COSMOtherm computed the fusion properties of individual components of the screened NADESs based on the solubility parameter. These properties were utilized in predictive modeling of solid–liquid equilibrium (SLE) plots by COSMOtherm, determining the eutectic melting temperature as a crucial parameter for assessing the feasibility of NADESs preparation under room-temperature conditions. Preparation of NADESs. Preparation of NADESs was conducted using a heating and stirring method. 40,41 Following the COSMO-therm-designed and screened NADESs combinations, components were meticulously weighed in a 1:1 molar ratio and mixed in a 250 mL round-bottomed flask. The mixture was then subjected to heating and stirring under a water bath at 70–80 °C, facilitated by a magnetic stirrer (DF-101S, China), until a clarified and transparent liquid was achieved. Subsequently, the solution was cooled to room temperature, allowing it to stand for 24 h while maintaining its clarified and transparent state, indicating the successful preparation of NADESs. **Determination of Experimental Solubility.** Actual solubility assessments were conducted by employing the saturated solution method. Specifically, 1 g of NADESSs was precisely weighed into a 2 mL plastic centrifuge tube. The appropriate quantity of the TFs 13150 https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c03110 ACS Sustainable Chem. Eng. 2024, 12, 13149–13162 ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering pubs.acs.org/journal/ascecg Research Article technicals was added incrementally to the NADESs, followed by 5 min of vortexing to ensure homogeneous dispersion and solubilization of the pesticides. The resulting mixture underwent ultrasonic (SY-500MD, China) treatment at room temperature for 30 min, promoting further dissolution until saturation was achieved. Subsequently, the solution underwent centrifugation (HC-2517, China) at 10,000 rpm for 1 min, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 µm organic membrane. It was then subjected to high-performance liquid chromatography (Agilent 1260) (HPLC) for the determination of actual solubility, and analytical methods are described in Table S1. Characterization of NADESs. Viscosity. The viscosity of the three most excellent dissolving ability NADESs (terpineol/decanoic acid 1:1, menthol/decanoic acid 1:1, and decyl alcohol/decanoic acid 1:1) was measured using a Brookfield DV1 viscometer (Bleafy). Thirty milliliters of each NADESS was placed in 50 mL plastic centrifuge tubes and subjected to a thermostatic water bath for 30 min. Viscosity measurements were then conducted at temperatures in the range of 20–60 °C. Each measurement was repeated three times. _Density_. The density of three NADESs was measured using a thermostatic liquid densitometer (DH-300L-T, China) over a temperature range of 20–60 C. Each treatment was repeated three times. *Refractive Index.* The refractive index (n_D) of the three NADESs was measured by using an Abbe refractometer (ABBE-3L) with a yellow beam at a wavelength of 589 nm. Measurements were taken at 25 ± 0.5 °C, and each treatment was repeated five times. The molar refraction was obtained from eq 1. R_D = \left(\frac{M}{\rho}\right)\left(\frac{n_D + 1}{n_D^2 + 1}\right) (1) where R_D, M, ρ, and n_D are molar refraction (cm³/mol), molar mass (g/mol), density (g/cm³), and refractive index, respectively. *Thermal Stability.* The thermal properties of the NADESs were assessed using a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) (NETZSCH, Germany). Approximately 10 mg of each sample was placed in an aluminum crucible and maintained at a constant temperature for 10 min under a nitrogen atmosphere. The temperature was then increased from -90 to 200 C at a constant rate of 10 C/min. Each treatment was repeated three times. Polarity. The Kamlet–Taft polarity parameters of the NADESs were determined using a UV–vis spectrophotometer (TU-1901, China).42 A solution comprising 0.05 mmol/L 4-nitroanisole, 0.05 mmol/L 4-nitroaniline, and 1 mmol/L Nile Red was initially prepared in methanol. Subsequently, 50 µL of the dye solution was added to a 2 mL centrifuge tube and dried under vacuum at 40 °C for 6 h to remove methanol. Following this, 1.0 g of NADESs was added to the centrifuge tube, vortexed to dissolve the dye, and ensured homogeneity with the staining dye. The adsorption spectra were then determined by using a UV–vis spectrophotometer. The Kamlet–Taft solute discoloration parameter was obtained from eqs 2 to 5. $\pi^* = 14.57 - 4270/\lambda_{\text{max, OMe}}$ (2) $\beta = 11.134 - 3580/\lambda_{\text{max, NH}_2} - 1.125\pi^*$ (3) $\alpha = (19.9657 - 1.0241 \times \pi^* - \nu_{\text{NR}})/1.6078$ (4) $\nu_{\text{NR}} = 1/(\lambda_{\text{max, NR}} \times 10^{-4})$ (5) where π*, α, and β denote the polarizability, hydrogen-giving capacity, and hydrogen-receiving capacity of the solvent, respectively. And the λ_max,OMe, λ_max,NH₂, and λ_max,NR represent the maximum absorption wavelengths of 4-nitroanisole, 4-nitroaniline, and Nile red, and ν_NR represents the maximum absorption wavenumber of Nile red. Dissolution Mechanism Studies. The dissolution mechanism was elucidated through MD simulations using GROMACS 2021.6 software suite. 43,44 The GROMOS96 54a7 United-Atom force field was employed to describe all molecules, 45 and the parameters for these molecules were sourced from the Automated Topology Builder Web site.⁴⁶,⁴⁷ TDF was selected as the model compound for the study, and MD simulations were conducted for three different ratios of the terpineol and decanoic acid solvent components. See Supporting Files for specific operations and parametrization of solvent simulation. The free energies of solvation of TDF in these three solvents were subsequently calculated. Quantum chemical calculations were carried out using the ORCA-5.0.4 program.⁴⁸ Geometry optimization and frequency calculations, as well as single- point energy calculations for each optimized geometry, were performed at higher energy levels employing wB97M-V/aug-cc- pVTZ to attain more accurate interaction energies and facilitate wave function analysis.⁴⁹ All electronic structure analyses were conducted using Multiwfn 3.8 (dev) program.⁵⁰ The energy and wave function analyses for visualizing the structures were performed using the VMD program.⁵¹ Application of TDF-NADESs Formulations. Preparation and Stability Assessment of TDF-NADESS. Referring to commercial EC formulations, TFs based on NADESs formulations with varying concentrations were separately prepared. The storage stability at elevated temperature of the AIs in six TFs was evaluated following the CIPAC MT46.3. These formulations were sealed in glass bottles and subjected to thermal storage in a constant temperature chamber at 54 ± 2 °C for 14 days. Subsequently, the samples were retrieved, placed in a desiccator, and cooled to room temperature, and the mass fraction of the AIs was determined. In Vitro Activity Assessment. The in vitro inhibitory activity of TDF-NADES systems against *Fusarium graminearum* was evaluated using the mycelial growth rate method. For instance, the formulation of 15% TDF based on three NADESs (terpineol/decanoic acid 1:1, menthol/decanoic acid 1:1, and decyl alcohol/decanoic acid 1:1) was prepared, with the 25% TDF commercial EC serving as a reference. *F. graminearum* cake (4 mm diameter) was inoculated into the center of potato dextrose agar (PDA) medium containing varying concentrations of TDF formulation, and sterile water was used as control treatment. The PDA medium was incubated at 28 ± 0.5 °C, and the mean diameter of mycelial growth was measured using the criss-cross method at 24, 48, and 72 h of incubation, respectively. Each treatment was replicated three times. The EC₅₀ was calculated by using the probit-log method. The inhibitory activity was expressed as mycelial growth inhibition (IR), which was obtained by eq 6. IR (%) = (D_0 - D_t) / (D_0 - 4) × 100 (6) where IR is mycelial growth inhibition. D₀ represents the diameter of control colonies (mm), Dₜ represents the diameter of treatment colonies (mm), and 4 represents the diameter of F. graminearum cake (mm). Wheat Leaf Adhesion. Fresh wheat leaves were chosen as the substrates for testing. The dynamic contact angle (DCA) of TDF-NADESs and the commercial EC on wheat leaves were measured using a contact angle meter (OCA50, Germany). The static contact angle at 120 s was considered the equilibrium contact angle of the droplets from the sample solution. Each experiment was conducted in quintuplicate. The equilibrium surface tension (EST) of TDF-NADESs and the EC solutions at various dilutions was determined using the Wilhelmy plate method with a tensiometer (DCAT 21, Germany). Each sample was analyzed in quintuplicate. The surface structure of wheat blades was characterized by using a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) (SU8100, Hitachi). To comprehensively assess adhesion and spreading abilities, the adhesion function of different solutions on wheat leaves was calculated based on the wetting equation, incorporating average values of EST at a 1000-fold dilution and the contact angle of droplets on wheat leaves at 120 s. The adhesion (Wₐ) was obtained from eq 7. W_a = \gamma(1 + \cos \theta) (7) where Wₐ is the work of adhesion (J/m²), γ is the EST of the pharmaceutical system (mN/m), and θ is the contact angle (deg). **Assessment of Wheat Safety.** Wheat seeds were soaked in distilled water for 4 h and then placed in Petri dishes (*d* = 15 cm) 13151 https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.4c03110 ACS Sustainable Chem. F. graminearum stands as the primary pathogen responsible for wheat scab, a highly destructive and challenging-to-control disease in agricultural production. The adherence of droplets to wheat leaves is pivotal for effective pesticide distribution and utilization. ⁶⁰ Figure 7a depicts the EST of TDF-NADESS and EC drops at varying dilutions, with field applications typically conducted at a 1000-fold dilution. At this concentration, the EST of the TDF-NADESs liquid was 14.5–15.6% lower than EC at the field application dilution, proving that the presence of NADESs contributed to a reduction in the EST of the formulation system. Additionally, the wettability of the formulation system on wheat leaves was evaluated through DCA measurements. As shown in Figure 7b, wheat leaf surfaces exhibited high hydrophobicity, evidenced by water's minimal wetting, with a DCA changing from 128 to 127° over 120 s. At a 1000-fold dilution, NADESs-based formulations exhibited 31.6–58.1% lower DCA, facilitating enhanced wetting and faster spreading on wheat leaves compared to EC. The hydrophobic component of wheat leaves primarily comprises a waxy layer, predominantly composed of sterols with chain lengths ranging from C20 to C32, where C28 is the dominant component. SEM revealed a microstructure with numerous folds, trichome structures, and a dense arrangement of waxy lamellar crystals, accentuating the leaf hydrophobicity (Figure 7f). This suggests that TDF-NADESs formulations hold promising applications in wheat and similar crops. CONCLUSIONS In this comprehensive investigation, COSMO-RS was utilized for the innovative design and high-throughput screening of novel NADESs with a superior solubilizing capacity for TDF. The reliability of COSMO-RS computational screening was corroborated by determining the actual solubility. The solubility of screened NADESs for TFs was enhanced by 2.8 × 10³ to 3.6 × 10⁵ times relative to water. This substantiated the universality of the screened NADESs against TDF for various TFs. Combining MD simulations, quantitative calculations, and properties, the critical factors and sites affecting the solvency of NADESs on TFs were identified as the hydrogen bonding between the triazole ring and hydroxyl group as well as the van der Waals force between benzene rings, which provided a foundational theoretical framework for future solvent design and screening endeavors. In addition, the properties of NADESs, such as viscosity, density, and polarity, also have a certain influence on their solubilization ability. Moreover, compared to conventional EC, the creation of eco-friendly TDF-NADESs formulation demonstrated enhanced in vitro inhibitory activity, superior adhesion, wetting abilities of wheat leaves, and lower EC₅₀ against F. graminearum. The interaction between NADESs components and leaf surface substances was systematically explored through calculations and characterization. Additionally, the pesticide systems of NADESs formulations exhibited diminished effects on wheat crop growth, lower cytotoxicity, and commendable biosafety. Leveraging the advantageous features of NADESs, such as natural components, high solubility, design flexibility, and the capacity to enhance pesticide utilization, holds tremendous promise for elevating pesticide efficiency, mitigating environmental pollution, and ushering in a new era of sustainable and efficient pesticides. Considering the pronounced acidic nature of LaA (Table S3), potentially limiting its practical applicability, our focus shifted to investigating NADESs based on DA in subsequent analyses. The solubilization capability of various DA-based NADESs, exhibiting different molar ratio variations, was initially explored for TDF. As depicted in Figure 2b, the solubilization efficacy of TDF increased gradually with increasing content of DA in the NADESs. This phenomenon could be attributed to the ability of DA to enhance the lipophilicity of the NADESs, thereby improving solubilization. Furthermore, the robust solubility observed in COSMO-RS screened NADESS for TDF extended to other TFs, namely, myclobutanil, hexaconazole, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, and propiconazole. Generally, the mobility of NADESs undergoes gradual changes, corresponding to variations in the ratio. In essence, higher DA ratios result in lower intermolecular interactions with Ter, leading to increased mobility. The optimization of this ratio holds potential for practical solvent carrier applications. Simulations were performed for Ter-DA with molar ratios of 1:1, 2:1, and 3:1. Diffusion coefficients for each substance in these three eutectic solvents were calculated, revealing that the mixtures with a 1:1 ratio exhibited the highest mobility (Table 3). Additionally, the densities of these solvents showed relatively small deviations from the experimental results, validating the force field parameters for these molecules. Subsequently, the determination of free energies of solubilization of TDF in each solvent was carried out through free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations to comprehend the impact of differences on solubility (Figure S1). In alignment with the experimental findings, the free energy of TDF dissolution gradually decreased with an increase in the Ter ratio in the solvent. Specifically, the Ter and DA ratio of 1:1 yielded the lowest free energy of dissolution (Table 3), signifying optimal solubilization of TDF in this solvent. In FEP calculations, Coulombic and van der Waals interactions were decoupled sequentially (Figure 4), elucidating the contribution of each interaction. The analysis revealed that van der Waals interactions predominantly governed dissolution; however, the decline in free energy of dissolution from 1:1 to 2:1 was primarily steered by Coulombic interactions. In-depth exploration of the interaction mode and strength between TDF and solvent molecules was conducted through quantum chemical calculations on a series of solvent–solvent dimers. These dimers were constructed via conformational searching for each monomer. Quantitative analysis of the molecular surface electrostatic potential (ESP) revealed consistently low values, even at the maximum or minimum points of the ESP (Figure 5a). Binding energies were computed, and three geometries representing the most stable binding configurations between TDF and each solvent molecule were selected for further analysis. The superposition of van der Waals surfaces of TDF and solvent molecule monomers in the dimeric structure is depicted in Figure 5b–d. Notably, the ESP-negative region around the TDF ideally overlapped with the ESP-positive region around the solvent molecule, whether it was DA or Ter. To ensure product quality, the stability of AIs in formulations is typically evaluated through hot storage stability tests. The thermal storage stability of TDF, along with myclobutanil, hexaconazole, tebuconazole, difenoconazole, and propiconazole, was assessed when it was dissolved in Ter-DA, Men-DA, DAch-DA, and Oct-DA using the CIPAC method. Both high and low concentrations maintained the stability of AIs, with content degradation before and after storage remaining below 5%. The formulations based on NADESs demonstrated the capacity to sustain the stability of product activity over a defined period (Figure S2). In Vitro Activity Evaluation. F. graminearum stands as the primary pathogen responsible for wheat scab, a highly destructive and challenging-to-control disease in agricultural production. Varied concentrations of TDF in Ter-DA, Men-DA, DAch-DA, and commercial EC were subjected to inhibitory activity assessments against F. graminearum, with results illustrated in Figure 6. The colony images in Figure 6a, captured at 72 h, demonstrate effective inhibition of F. graminearum growth across concentrations ranging from 6.25 to 200 mg/L. Figure 6b showed images of colony growth at different times under treatment with the concentration applied in the field (200 mg/L). The concentration-dependent inhibitory effects of TDF formulations were evident, showing a substantial increase in inhibition rates with increasing concentrations (Figure 6c-e). TDF-NADESs exhibited significantly higher inhibitory effects compared to EC. For instance, at 24 h, the inhibition rate for TDF EC was 53.2% at the lowest concentration (6.25 mg/L) and 92.6% at the highest concentration (200 mg/L). In contrast, TDF-NADESs achieved rates of 60.2 and 93.7%, respectively, indicating increased bactericidal activity in the presence of NADESs. Furthermore, the inhibitory effect at concentrations below 100 mg/L gradually decreased with an extended treatment time. However, at higher concentrations, not only did the inhibitory effect remain unaffected but it also exhibited an enhancement. EC50 values at 24 h for EC, Ter-DA, Men-DA, and DAch-DA were 5.252, 3.864, 4.589, and 3.848 mg/L, respectively, indicating superior activities of TDF-NADES formulations (Table 4). In conclusion, TDF-NADES formulations exhibited excellent in vitro bacterial inhibitory activities, showcasing significant potential for practical applications in agriculture. Adhesion of TDF-NADESS on Wheat Leaves. The adherence of droplets to wheat leaves is pivotal for effective pesticide distribution and utilization. ⁶⁰ Figure 7a depicts the EST of TDF-NADESS and EC drops at varying dilutions, with field applications typically conducted at a 1000-fold dilution. At this concentration, the EST of the TDF-NADESs liquid was 14.5–15.6% lower than EC at the field application dilution, proving that the presence of NADESs contributed to a reduction in the EST of the formulation system. Additionally, the wettability of the formulation system on wheat leaves was evaluated through DCA measurements. As shown in Figure 7b, wheat leaf surfaces exhibited high hydrophobicity, evidenced by water's minimal wetting, with a DCA changing from 128 to 127° over 120 s. At a 1000-fold dilution, NADESs-based formulations exhibited 31.6–58.1% lower DCA, facilitating enhanced wetting and faster spreading on wheat leaves compared to EC. As shown in Figure 7c, the adhesion work of EC was 14.9 mJ/m², while Ter-DA, Men-DA, and DAch-DA exhibited higher values of 35.3, 28.2, and 30.4 mJ/m², respectively. This underscores that TDF-NADESs formulations exhibited supe- rior adhesion to hydrophobic wheat leaves, enhancing solution utilization. The hydrophobic component of wheat leaves primarily comprises a waxy layer, predominantly composed of sterols with chain lengths ranging from C20 to C32, where C28 is the dominant component. SEM revealed a microstructure with numerous folds, trichome structures, and a dense arrangement of waxy lamellar crystals, accentuating the leaf hydrophobicity (Figure 7f). The intermolecular interactions between C28 sterols and NADESs and conventional solvents (benzene, toluene, and xylene) were calculated using a COMO-RS simulation (Figure 7e,g). The results indicated that NADESs exhibited stronger van der Waals forces and readily formed intermolecular hydrogen bonds with C28 sterols. This suggests that TDF-NADESs formulations hold promising applications in wheat and similar crops. Leveraging the morphology, microstructure, and composition of target crop leaves, cosolvents for active ingredients can be designed and screened using COSMO-RS, providing a simplified and effective approach for future pesticide formulation design and preparation. Wheat, being highly susceptible to environ- mental variations, experiences growth inhibitory effects due to external environmental resistance and stress factors. 32 Assess- ing the biosafety of TDF-NADESS involves measuring wheat growth indicators. Figures 8 and S1 depict the influence of EC and NADESs formulations on wheat growth at the field application concentration. Seven days postapplication, NA- DESs formulations treatments displayed no significant inhibitory effects on wheat, with no considerable impact on root length, stem dry weight, and fresh weight. This sensitivity might be attributed to the predominant retention of the sprayed solution in the soil, exerting a more pronounced effect on the root growth. The CCK-8 method was employed to test mouse fibroblasts L929, with the aim of assessing the biosafety of NADESs formulations. Test results (Figure 9) revealed that, in comparison to the control group, the cell survival rates for NADES formulations at a concentration of 100 mg/L were notably high 24 h post-treatment of L929, registering at 92.8–96.9%. CONCLUSIONS In this comprehensive investigation, COSMO-RS was utilized for the innovative design and high-throughput screening of novel NADESs with a superior solubilizing capacity for TDF. The reliability of COSMO-RS computational screening was corroborated by determining the actual solubility. The solubility of screened NADESs for TFs was enhanced by 2.8 × 10³ to 3.6 × 10⁵ times relative to water. This substantiated the universality of the screened NADESs against TDF for various TFs. Combining MD simulations, quantitative calculations, and properties, the critical factors and sites affecting the solvency of NADESs on TFs were identified as the hydrogen bonding between the triazole ring and hydroxyl group as well as the van der Waals force between benzene rings, which provided a foundational theoretical framework for future solvent design and screening endeavors. In addition, the properties of NADESs, such as viscosity, density, and polarity, also have a certain influence on their solubilization ability. Moreover, compared to conventional EC, the creation of eco-friendly TDF-NADESs formulation demonstrated enhanced in vitro inhibitory activity, superior adhesion, wetting abilities of wheat leaves, and lower EC₅₀ against F. graminearum. The interaction between NADESs components and leaf surface substances was systematically explored through calculations and characterization. Additionally, the pesticide systems of NADESs formulations exhibited diminished effects on wheat crop growth, lower cytotoxicity, and commendable biosafety. Leveraging the advantageous features of NADESs, such as natural components, high solubility, design flexibility, and the capacity to enhance pesticide utilization, holds tremendous promise for elevating pesticide efficiency, mitigating environmental pollution, and ushering in a new era of sustainable and efficient pesticides.
